category_title: Students who disrupt instruction to avoid difficult independent tasks
minimal_context: Jay is sitting at his desk in his third-grade classroom as the teacher directs the class to begin their independent math practice worksheet.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Alright everyone, we've finished going over the new math concepts. It's time to begin your independent practice on the worksheet at your desks.

STUDENT: (Fails to attempt his individual seatwork and blurts out loudly) This is too hard! I'm not doing this!

TUTOR: Jay, please focus on your own paper and try to start the first problem.

STUDENT: (Bellows across the room) I said I don't know how to do it! It's impossible!

TUTOR: Just do your best and keep trying.

STUDENT: (Persistently calls out and bellows, causing disruptions to the point where other students complain, while still failing to attempt the seatwork) I need help! You have to show me! I'm not doing it!

options.A: Provide the student with access to similar, but more socially appropriate, sensory stimulation by giving him a squishy stress-relief ball.
options.B: Review antecedent data from the math class to create a hypothesis statement that includes the perceived reason for the behavior.
options.C: Implement relatively tight timelines for the student to complete the independent math practice worksheet during the class session.
options.D: Conduct scaffolding conversations in chunks over the course of the math lesson, coming and going before resuming the next part.
